title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging and Stimulation in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation: A Review

subsections.section_title: Brain Imaging Methods for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) for Mapping Motor Cortex Plasticity and Oscillatory Dynamics
subsections.content:
Brain imaging is an important achievement of modern science, and it is thriving. With the improvement of temporal and spatial resolution of brain imaging techniques, as well as the integration of multimodal imaging methods, the observation scale of the brain is becoming wider, which is conducive to the research of brain science and the treatment of brain diseases. This section introduces the application of EEG, MEG, fMRI, fNIRS, and multimodal imaging in the motor function assessment of stroke. Fig. 1 shows the equipment for the four imaging modalities and the preliminary visualization results of the collected data.

Each imaging method has its advantages and disadvantages, and multimodal imaging can complement these advantages to provide a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of changes in brain structure and function ref [110]. We examined research reports from the last decade and found that the most popular multimodal combinations are EEG-fMRI ref [111] and EEG-fNIRS ref [112], ref [113]. EEG-MEG ref [56] and fMRI-fNIRS ref [114] combined studies have also been performed, but few studies have explored motor function assessment after stroke. EEG or MEG and EMG coupling analysis is another popular multimodal analysis method that can establish a correlation between brain activity and muscle behavior, which has unique advantages in assessing motor loss caused by abnormal neural activity after stroke ref [115]. This section focuses on applying EEG-fMRI coupling, EEG-FNRIS coupling, and EEG-EMG coupling in motor function assessment of stroke.

subsections.section_title: Brain Imaging Methods for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: fNIRS for Non-Invasive Monitoring of Cortical Activation and Connectivity in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
EEG is a general reflection of the electrical activity of brain nerve cells in the scalp ref [27]. With a time resolution of milliseconds, it can record faster brain activity ref [10]. However, the spatial resolution of EEG is limited because it is necessary to place an electrode with a diameter of about 1 cm on the scalp ref [28]. With the development of high-density EEG and source location technology, EEG has shown unique advantages in the field of diagnosis and evaluation of brain diseases ref [29], ref [30]. EEG electrode positioning is based on the standard 10-20 system, which currently achieves up to 256 channels ref [31]. Before a further state analysis, source localization analysis of raw EEG signals is required, that is, inverse estimation of the location, direction, and intensity of neural activity sources in the brain. Source localization analysis software includes MATLAB plugins, such as Brainstorm, EEGLAB, FieldTrip, NutMeg, and SPM, as well as independent analysis software, such as MNE, OpenMEEG, and NeuroFEM ref [32].

There is a certain degree of information transmission and interaction between the cerebral cortex and the muscles during limb motion ref [115]. Corticomuscular coupling (CMC) is a quantitative assessment method that can reflect cerebral cortex information and motor muscle state ref [132]. CMC reveals the FC between the cerebral cortex and muscles by quantifying the synchronization between EMG ref [133] and EEG ref [134], or MEG ref [135]. The CMC phenomenon between the central nervous system and the periphery nervous system is essential for the neural control of movement. This functional coupling between the brain and muscle originates from the neural signal afferent and efferent process ref [136]. The brain transmits control commands to the peripheral nervous system in electrical charges through interconnected synapses and neuronal cells and then controls the contraction or extension of various muscle groups. The afferent process is a reverse process, and the feedback signal comes from the proprioceptors of muscles or joints and the mechanoreceptors of the skin ref [137]. Based on the complex interaction between the cortex and muscles at different coupling levels, CMC can be roughly divided into linear coupling and nonlinear coupling. Linear coupling analysis methods are mainly based on amplitude squared coherence, short-time Fourier time-frequency coherence, wavelet coherence, Granger causality, partial directed coherence, etc. The nonlinear coupling analysis method is mainly based on nonlinear Granger causality, mutual information, cross-spectral coherence, multispectral phase coherence, transfer entropy estimation, etc.

subsections.section_title: Brain Imaging Methods for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: fMRI and Functional Connectivity for Tracking Cortical Reorganization During Motor Recovery
subsections.content:
MEG records neural activity by measuring changes in the brain's magnetic field using a sensitive magnetometer with a spatial resolution better than EEG ref [53], ref [54], ref [55]. However, MEG is easily interfered with by environmental magnetic fields when measuring small magnetic field changes ref [56]. MEG has become a means of stroke assessment or other brain disease detection because the spatial resolution has been further improved with the increase of the number of sensors, and the source location algorithm has also been extensively developed ref [16]. More than 250 channels of MEG signal can be collected simultaneously. MEG and EEG are different manifestations of the same signal, so analysis software is common to both. The difficulty of collecting MEG signals is that the magnetic field generated by brain activity is the pT degree, more than 100 times weaker than the Earth's magnetic field. MEG's recording was made possible by the invention of a sensitive magnetic flux detector called superconducting quantum interference device ref [57].

Functional MRI (fMRI) enables in vivo assessment of the spatial and temporal patterns of functional and structural changes inside and outside ischemic lesion areas, contributing to the elucidation of critical aspects in post-stroke brain remodeling ref [3]. Task/stimulus-related fMRI, resting-state fMRI, and pharmacological MRI allow direct or indirect measurement of neuronal activation, functional connectivity, or neurotransmitter system responses, respectively ref [3]. Resting-state fMRI, which does not require patient effort, has been used to elucidate the disruption of functional connections within hours of ischemic stroke and to track recovery dynamics ref [7]. Longitudinal studies have demonstrated that resting-state functional connectivity of the ipsilesional primary motor cortex (M1) changes over time after stroke, with increased connectivity to frontal, parietal, thalamic, and cerebellar regions, and decreased connectivity to the contralesional M1 and occipital cortex ref [8]. The asymmetry in interhemispheric functional connectivity between M1 regions is most pronounced at 1 month post-stroke and correlates with motor recovery outcomes at 6 months ref [8]. Furthermore, the functional connectivity between the ipsilesional M1 and contralesional dorsal premotor area at the acute stage independently predicts functional outcome at 3 months ref [10]. The balance of hemispheric activation in the primary motor cortex, measured via laterality index, remains correlated with motor deficit throughout recovery, suggesting a persistent role of interhemispheric imbalance ref [12]. Altered effective connectivity of the primary motor cortex, assessed using Granger causality analysis in resting-state fMRI, reveals directional changes in network interactions that are disrupted after stroke ref [14]. Together, these fMRI and functional connectivity methods provide an unprecedented means to measure longitudinal changes in tissue function, evaluate neural network organization, and identify degenerative and restorative processes affecting motor recovery ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Brain Imaging Methods for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: EEG-Based Assessment of Motor Recovery and Brain Symmetry in Stroke
subsections.content:
fMRI is a nonradioactive technique that looks at brain activity based on blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) and has been widely used in neuroscience ref [66]. Changes in movement-related BOLD activation patterns during stroke rehabilitation provide evidence for the use of fMRI in rehabilitation assessment ref [67]. The prediction of motor rehabilitation combined with fMRI showed an increase in explanation compared to the FMA score alone ref [68]. Interhemispheric activation balance in motor-related cortex changes with the rehabilitation process and laterality indexes (LIs) before and after the improvement of motor function can be a good measurement ref [69], ref [70]. The equation LIs = (ipsilesional activation − contralesional activation) / (ipsilesional activation + contralesional activation). LIs range from −1 to 1, with +1 representing complete ipsilesional activation and −1 representing exclusively contralesional activation. Contralaterality index (CI) is essentially the same indicator as LIs, and its equation CI = (contralesional − ipsilesional) / (contralesional + ipsilesional), which is used in some reports ref [71]. fMRI analysis in kinematics showed that a larger area of the cortex was activated when the patient performed ankle dorsal plantar-flexion movements one month after the rehabilitation evaluation ref [72]. After six months of rehabilitation, the activation balance in the patient's primary motor cortex shifted to the affected hemisphere ref [73]. Longitudinal evaluation of brain activation balance changes from onset to several months post-stroke by fMRI can effectively evaluate the rehabilitation therapy ref [74], ref [75]. Two weeks after treatment with constraint-induced movement therapy, fMRI activation in the sensorimotor area increased significantly, and the magnitude was greater in ipsilesional than contralesional ref [76].

EEG-based assessments have emerged as valuable tools for evaluating motor recovery and brain symmetry in stroke patients. Dense-array EEG has been shown to capture acute stroke behavioral deficits with high correlation to NIHSS scores, reflecting its utility in clinical assessment ref [12]. The Brain Symmetry Index (BSI), derived from spectral analysis of EEG signals, has been widely used to detect interhemispheric asymmetry in acute ischemic stroke, with elevated BSI values consistently indicating pathological asymmetry ref [15]. The revised Brain Symmetry Index (r-BSI) has demonstrated significant correlation with short-term functional prognosis, as measured by Barthel Index and modified Rankin Scale, establishing its prognostic value ref [18]. A bilateral brain symmetry index (BBSI) has been proposed to improve uniformity and reliability in distinguishing stroke patients from healthy controls, showing increased values with worsening prognosis ref [19]. In chronic stroke, quantitative EEG measures including BSI and Delta/Alpha Ratio (DAR) have been correlated with upper-limb motor recovery outcomes following robot-assisted rehabilitation, suggesting their predictive utility ref [17]. Furthermore, BSI has been found to be significantly higher in stroke patients compared to healthy controls, with stronger differences observed in cortical stroke subgroups, and has shown mild but persistent correlation with Fugl-Meyer assessment scores ref [9]. EEG features such as DAR, DTABR, and BSI have been successfully used as input features for machine learning models to classify acute ischemic stroke severity with high accuracy, demonstrating their potential as automated diagnostic tools ref [15]. A 1D convolutional neural network applied to EEG power spectral density features achieved 97.3% accuracy in classifying stroke severity into normal, mild, moderate, and severe categories, highlighting the power of deep learning in EEG-based stroke assessment ref [16].

subsections.subsection_title: Corticomuscular Coherence and Multimodal Integration for Motor Output Assessment
subsections.content: fNIRS is an emerging brain imaging technology in recent years. Its principle is similar to fMRI, that is, neural activity in the brain can lead to changes in hemodynamics ref [94], ref [95]. Oxygenated hemoglobin and deoxygenated hemoglobin in brain tissue have different absorption rates of near-infrared light to varying wavelengths of 600-900 nm, which can be deduced to the brain activity according to the Beer-Lambert law ref [96]. Furthermore, the spatial resolution of fNIRS as fMRI is far superior to that of EEG and MEG. Meanwhile, the time sampling rate of fNIRS can reach about 10 Hz, which is higher than that of fMRI ref [97].

subsections.section_title: Brain Stimulation Techniques in Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
Brain stimulation has evolved from invasive electrode stimulation to implantable and noninvasive stimulation. In recent years, with the development of noninvasive brain stimulation ref [150], the clinical application of TMS ref [151], and tDCS ref [152] has achieved good results in the stroke motor rehabilitation. The mechanism of how TMS and tDCS contribute to stroke motor rehabilitation has yet to be confirmed. Feasible mechanisms include hemispheric interaction inhibition ref [153], change of neuronal membrane potential polarity ref [154] and brain plasticity ref [155]. The TMS and tDCS affect not only the target areas of the motor cortex but also affect the networks of the brain and spinal cord that are connected at a distance ref [156]. Typical tDCS and TMS devices are shown in Fig. 4. In this section, we will review the research on the application and mechanism of TMS and tDCS in stroke motor rehabilitation within the last ten years.

Rehabilitation: tDCS has been increasingly used as an adjunct therapy for motor rehabilitation, but its potential application is limited because of the unclear mechanism of action ref [187]. The current explanation for the means of tDCS can be summarized as changing the polarity of neuronal membrane potential and regulating synaptic plasticity. The underlying mechanism of tDCS has been studied since the 1960s, and it was proved that tDCS could change cortical excitability by detecting the change of motor-evoked potential through TMS in 1998 ref [188]. When weak direct current is applied to the scalp, the resting membrane potential and spontaneous discharge rate of neurons are modulated, leading to plasticity ref [154]. Anodal tDCS causes neurons membrane to depolarize, leading to an increase in the excitability of the cortex, while cathodal tDCS causes neurons membrane to polarize to decrease excitability ref [189]. The membrane potential polarization state change may be the mechanism of effect after tDCS. TDCS can induce long-lasting changes in synaptic excitability in the motor cortex, and the biological agent is LTP and LTD phenomena at the cellular level ref [166]. Some studies suggest that tDCS induces synaptic plasticity by altering changes in neurotransmitter concentration ref [188]. Moreover, some studies have shown that anodic tDCS can reduce gamma-aminobutyric acid in the cortex and enhance cortical excitability. On the contrary, cathode tDCS reduced glutamate concentration and thus reduced cortical excitability ref [190]. Studies have shown that weak tDCS can produce sustained excitability. Both anodal and cathodal tDCS increased the affected M1 motor-evoked potential in stroke patients ref [191]. The after effect of tDCS also reflected in reducing the inhibitory effect from CL to IL ref [192]. In addition, changes in dopamine, acetylcholine, and serotonin may also be involved, but more research is needed to confirm this ref [188].

subsections.section_title: Brain Stimulation Techniques in Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
TMS is painless stimulation of the cerebral cortex or peripheral nerves divided into single-pulse TMS and repetitive TMS (rTMS). Single-pulse TMS is usually used in combination with other imaging methods to assess motor function after stroke, while rTMS is used for motor rehabilitation treatment ref [1]. The magnetic field passes unattenuated through high-impedance tissues, such as the skull and scalp, causing the cerebral cortex to generate induced currents. Induced currents change the membrane potential of cells, increasing or inhibiting the excitability of neurons. Changes in neuronal excitability can affect synaptic plasticity and promote motor learning and motor function recovery after stroke ref [5]. According to the size of stimulus frequency, rTMS can be divided into low-frequency stimulation (≤ 1 Hz) and high-frequency stimulation (> 1 Hz). Low-frequency rTMS can reduce the excitability of the target cortex, while high-frequency rTMS can improve it ref [1].

Brain stimulation has been proved to be effective in the rehabilitation of motor function after stroke. However, most brain stimulation methods are open loop, requiring the physician to close the loop through the stimulation parameters and the patient's behavioral outcome. Some studies combine brain stimulation with brain imaging to achieve controlled regulation of brain activity. Brain stimulation enables temporal and spatial alterations in brain networks, and brain imaging assesses functional implications resulting from these alterations ref [1], ref [5]. Through the combination, the interaction between different components of the brain network and their respective functional role can be explored, so as to form a more detailed evaluation of brain functional network ref [5]. Some studies have also combined TMS with EEG, fMRI and other imaging techniques to monitor brain activity with higher temporal and spatial resolution, so as to realize the prediction of motor recovery after stroke ref [5]. The common use of EEG cap provides a basis for the study of EEG combined with tDCS. The immediate and after effects of tDCS were demonstrated by changes in the characteristics of CMC and EEG signals ref [1].

subsections.section_title: Brain Stimulation Techniques in Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) for Motor Recovery
subsections.content: Current studies generally believe that the mechanism of rTMS for stroke rehabilitation is reflected in the modulation of hemispheric interaction ref [26] and enhancement of brain plasticity ref [25]. It has been shown in the previous section that stroke can lead to disruption of the activation balance between the cerebral hemispheres. The excitability of the motion-related areas on the ipsilesional hemisphere decreased, but the contralesional hemisphere's excitability increased. In addition, when the affected hand performed motor tasks, the contralesional hemisphere inhibited the ipsilesional hemisphere. High-frequency TMS can improve the excitability of the motor cortex of the ipsilesional, but low-frequency TMS can inhibit the excitability of the motor cortex of the contralesional, thus realizing the regulation of cerebral hemisphere interaction ref [28], ref [11]. After treatment with rTMS, the lateralization of power spectral density and information transmission efficiency between bilateral hemispheric central cortexes was significantly changed. In other words, rTMS can modulate hemispheric lateralization, which may be an important neural mechanism to improve motor function ref [13], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Brain Stimulation Techniques in Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) for Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.content: tDCS is a type of transcranial electrical stimulation that regulates the excitability of neurons by applying a weak direct current to the cerebral cortex ref [31]. tDCS can be divided into anodal tDCS and cathodal tDCS according to the polarity of the electrodes applied to the target stimulated brain region. In general, anodal tDCS can enhance the excitability of the target area, while cathodal tDCS can inhibit it ref [6], ref [7], ref [8]. The current ranging from 0.5 to 2 mA poses no risk to the human body, with a single session lasting from 7 to 40 min. Common electrode pads are 15-35 cm² in size, so the current density is about 0.04-0.06 mA/cm². Typically, the moderating effects of tDCS last from a few minutes to several hours after the stimulation ref [31], ref [8], ref [14]. After a single session of 20-30 min, the effect can last about 90 min. After five consecutive days of stimulation, the aftereffect lasted for three months. Compared to rTMS, tDCS is more portable and safe, with less patient discomfort, and can be easily combined with other peripheral therapies ref [31], ref [8], ref [14].

subsections.subsection_title: Combined tDCS and Robotic Therapy for Upper Limb Recovery
subsections.content: The use of brain imaging provides a more accurate solution to the precise assessment of motor function post-stroke, which is the basis of navigated rehabilitation. To better characterize brain function networks, high spatial, and temporal resolution imaging techniques are required. Multimodal imaging can make up for the defect of single mode and will become the mainstream research direction in the future. EEG-fMRI and EEG-fNIRS have attracted much attention and obtained some research results, and can further explore their potential in the future. CMC is a novel evaluation method that can get information about muscle states and brain states. It provides a correlation between the brain and muscles (which reflects the brain's ability to control muscles) and provides time delay information (which reflects changes in information transmission), which is helpful for assessing motor function after stroke. Graph theory can supplement traditional statistical analysis and is very important for building brain networks. A number of features can be extracted that are more indicative of change before and after treatment, which are essential for quantifying recovery progress. The evaluation method based on brain imaging can well supplement the deficiency of the clinical qualitative evaluation scale.

Although rTMS and tDCS are effective in rebuilding motor function post-stroke, there are no guidelines for clinical use. The safe range of brain stimulation parameters should pay attention, which is crucial to whether patients accept treatment. Effective stimulation processes and paradigms need to be explored, which is the focus of current research. Brain stimulation combined with other interventions proved to be more effective and more acceptable to stroke patients. Combined augmented reality-based training can significantly increase muscle activity and strength of chronic phase stroke patients compared to EMG-triggered functional electric stimulation alone ref [37]. Functional electric stimulation and robotic-assisted training can achieve shoulder, elbow, and wrist complex upper limb movements ref [214]. The study preliminarily proved that bilateral tDCS to robot-assisted therapy have significant rehabilitation effects on stroke patients, and there are significant differences in patients with different stroke stages and types ref [215]. Vision restoration training combined with tDCS may be better than standard vision training for rehabilitation, but this conclusion needs further proof ref [216]. Brain stimulation improves brain plasticity more than traditional physical training, but the combination of the two is more effective in restoring brain and muscle function.

This article emphasizes the importance of assessment for rehabilitation, and the combination of noninvasive brain imaging and brain stimulation is the future direction. After an accurate assessment of the cerebral functional network, hemispheric balance index, and CMC characteristic values of stroke patients, the brain stimulation paradigm formulation can improve rehabilitation efficiency and make the therapy closed-loop ref [38]. A simultaneous tDCS-EEG study demonstrated that tDCS can modulate the synchronization of cortical rhythms during and after administration ref [15]. Simultaneous use of tDCS and EEG-EMG system demonstrated that stroke patients had the greatest changes in CMC under anode tDCS, with the greatest effect occurring 10-min after stimulation ref [38]. The efficacy of rTMS was evaluated by fMRI and the results were consistent with the clinical evaluation ref [2]. Researchers used rTMS in combination with EEG-EMG system demonstrated that rTMS can improve motor function by constructing a brain-muscle network, which providing us with a new research perspective ref [38]. Closed-loop studies of neuromodulation-based rehabilitation methods can explore safe and effective stimulus parameters to promote their use in clinical rehabilitation ref [38]. Due to the limitation of equipment and experimental conditions, the combined research of some brain imaging and brain stimulation methods has not formed a closed loop. However, this should be the focus of future research.

subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal Stimulation: tDCS with Vision and Sensory Training
subsections.content: Exercise rehabilitation after stroke is affected by sociodemographic characteristics (such as age, gender, race, etc.), clinical factors (such as stroke type, co-morbidities, rehabilitation therapeutics, etc.), and genetic factors ref [219]. As a result, there is a significant difference in stroke patients, which requires the establishment of individualized rehabilitation therapies. More effective than scale assessment, brain imaging technology can be used to establish the state of the individual brain functional network for each patient so that personalized brain stimulation rehabilitation therapy can be built. Fatigue is a common syndrome after stroke, which will directly affect the results of motor function assessment and intervention. Fatigue manifestations in stroke patients include brain fatigue and muscle fatigue. Taking fatigue into account when constructing a patient's brain functional network is a grand challenge, as in brain stimulation treatment. The assessment and treatment of post-stroke fatigue have attracted the attention of researchers, and brain imaging and brain stimulation techniques can also become effective means.

This article summarizes state of art in brain imaging and stimulation, exploring potential solutions to post-stroke motor rehabilitation. The principle, advantages, limitations, and analytical methods of EEG, MEG, fMRI, and fNIRS brain imaging were presented with the intent of demonstrating the benefits of brain imaging in the motor function assessment of stroke. We summarized the application of rTMS and tDCS in stroke rehabilitation, the setting of stimulus parameters, and their mechanism. More studies are needed in the future to demonstrate its effectiveness in motor rehabilitation and to identify clinical stimulation paradigms. Finally, we discussed the prospects of combining brain imaging with brain stimulation in stroke rehabilitation, which we believe will be the direction of future research. Based on the summary of motor rehabilitation of stroke, there are typical problems in motor impairment caused by neurological diseases, such as spinal injury and epilepsy. It is expected that this article would facilitate researchers and practitioners with a better understanding of noninvasive brain imaging and brain stimulation and their development on solutions to post-stroke motor rehabilitation.
